items.title: 13.4 Derivation of x^n where n in Z

blocks.text: (a) We find the derivative of \(x^{n}\) when \(n\) is positive integer.

(a) Let \(y = x^{n}\). Then
\[y + \delta y = (x + \delta x)^{n}\]
and
\[\delta y = (x + \delta x)^{n} - x^{n}\]

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the label "(a)" twice in a row: once before "We find the derivative of \(x^{n}\) when \(n\) is positive integer" and again before "Let \(y = x^{n}\)". Both lines belong to the same part (a); the second label is a repeat. Part (b) (negative integers) follows on the next page.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
This is exactly the four-step method of 13.3.2 with a general power \(n\): Step I gives \(y + \delta y\), Step II gives \(\delta y\). The only new tool is the binomial theorem, which expands \((x + \delta x)^{n}\) for any positive integer \(n\):
\[(x+\delta x)^{n} = x^{n} + nx^{n-1}\delta x\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{n-2}(\delta x)^{2} + \ldots + (\delta x)^{n}\]
The book writes \(2!\) in the old notation \(\underline{|2}\); both mean \(2 \times 1 = 2\).

Using the binomial theorem, we have
\[\delta y = \Big[x^{n} + nx^{n-1}\cdot\delta x\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{n-2}(\delta x)^{2} + \ldots\]
\[+ (\delta x)^{n}\Big] - x^{n}\]

i.e.,
\[\delta y = \delta x\Big[nx^{n-1}\]
\[+ \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{n-2}\cdot\delta x + \ldots\]
\[+ (\delta x)^{n-1}\Big] \quad \text{(i)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: How do we get (i)? The first term \(x^{n}\) cancels with \(-x^{n}\). Every remaining term has at least one factor \(\delta x\), so we take one \(\delta x\) outside the bracket; each power of \(\delta x\) inside drops by one.

Dividing both sides of (i) by \(\delta x\), gives
\[\dfrac{\delta y}{\delta x} = nx^{n-1} + \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{n-2}\cdot\delta x\]
\[+ \ldots + (\delta x)^{n-1} \quad \text{(ii)}\]

Note that each term on the right hand side of (ii) involves \(\delta x\) except the first term, so taking the limit as \(\delta x \to 0\), we get
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = nx^{n-1}\]
As \(y = x^{n}\), so
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{n}) = n\cdot x^{n-1}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Check the formula against Section 13.3.2: for \(n = 2\) it gives \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) = 2x\), the answer of Example 3(b). For \(n = 3\) it gives \(3x^{2}\), and expanding \((x+\delta x)^{3}\) by hand gives the same.

(b) Let \(y = x^{n}\) where \(n\) is negative integer.
Let \(n = -m\) (\(m\) is a positive integer). Then
\[y = x^{-m} = \dfrac{1}{x^{m}} \quad \text{(i)}\]
\[y + \delta y = \dfrac{1}{(x+\delta x)^{m}} \quad \text{(ii)}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why put \(n = -m\)? The binomial expansion used in (a) works for positive integer powers. Writing \(x^{n} = \frac{1}{x^{m}}\) with \(m > 0\) lets us use that expansion again, this time for \((x+\delta x)^{m}\) in the denominator. We need \(x \ne 0\) here.

Subtracting (i) from (ii), gives
\[\delta y = \dfrac{1}{(x+\delta x)^{m}} - \dfrac{1}{x^{m}}\]
\[= \dfrac{x^{m}-(x+\delta x)^{m}}{x^{m}(x+\delta x)^{m}}\]
Expanding \((x + \delta x)^{m}\) by binomial theorem, the numerator is
\[x^{m}-(x+\delta x)^{m}\]
\[= x^{m} - \Big[x^{m} + mx^{m-1}\delta x\]
\[+ \dfrac{m(m-1)}{2!}x^{m-2}(\delta x)^{2}\]
\[+ \ldots + (\delta x)^{m}\Big]\]
\[= -\delta x\Big[mx^{m-1}\]
\[+ \dfrac{m(m-1)}{2!}x^{m-2}\delta x\]
\[+ \ldots + (\delta x)^{m-1}\Big]\]
so
\[\delta y = \dfrac{-\delta x\big[mx^{m-1} + \ldots\big]}{x^{m}(x+\delta x)^{m}}\]

and
\[\dfrac{\delta y}{\delta x} = \dfrac{-1}{x^{m}(x+\delta x)^{m}}\]
\[\cdot\Big(mx^{m-1} + \dfrac{m(m-1)}{2!}x^{m-2}\cdot\delta x\]
\[+ \ldots + (\delta x)^{m-1}\Big)\]

Taking limit when \(\delta x \to 0\), we get (all terms containing \(\delta x\) vanish)
\[\dfrac{dy}{dx} = \dfrac{-1}{x^{m}\cdot x^{m}}\cdot mx^{m-1}\]
\[= -mx^{m-1}\cdot x^{-2m}\]
\[= -mx^{(-m)-1}\]
\[= nx^{n-1} \quad [\because -m = n]\]
or
\[\dfrac{d(x)^{n}}{dx} = nx^{n-1}\]

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The steps after the limit use only the laws of indices:
\(\frac{1}{x^{m}\cdot x^{m}} = \frac{1}{x^{2m}} = x^{-2m}\), and \(x^{m-1}\cdot x^{-2m} = x^{m-1-2m} = x^{-m-1}\).
Finally \(-m = n\), so \(-mx^{-m-1} = nx^{n-1}\): the same formula as in part (a).

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{n}) = nx^{n-1}\) is called power rule. Where \(n \in \mathbb{R}\).

So, we have proved that \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{n}) = nx^{n-1}\), if \(n \in \mathbb{Z}\).
The above rule also holds if \(n \in \mathbb{Q} - \mathbb{Z}\), i.e. for rational powers.
For example,
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{2}{3}}\right) = \dfrac{2}{3}x^{\frac{2}{3}-1}\]
\[= \dfrac{2}{3x^{\frac{1}{3}}}\]
The proof of \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{n}) = nx^{n-1}\) when \(n \in \mathbb{Q} - \mathbb{Z}\) is left as an exercise.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
What has been proved here? Only integer powers: (a) positive integers, (b) negative integers. The case \(n = 0\) is also covered: \(x^{0} = 1\) is a constant, and \(\frac{d}{dx}(1) = 0 = 0\cdot x^{-1}\) (Example 3(a)). For rational and real powers the book only states the rule.
For fractional powers the rule is used where \(x^{n}\) and \(x^{n-1}\) are defined; for example \(x^{\frac{1}{2}} = \sqrt{x}\) needs \(x > 0\) for its derivative.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Using the power rule (our examples, checked against the first-principles results):
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{5}) = 5x^{4}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{-3}) = -3x^{-4} = \dfrac{-3}{x^{4}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}\right) = \dfrac{d}{dx}(x^{-2}) = \dfrac{-2}{x^{3}}\]
\[\dfrac{d}{dx}(\sqrt{x}) = \dfrac{d}{dx}\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}\right) = \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}\]
The last two agree with Examples 5 and 4, which were done by definition.

blocks.title: Exam tip
blocks.text: Before using the power rule, write roots and reciprocals as powers: \(\sqrt[3]{x} = x^{\frac{1}{3}}\), \(\frac{1}{x^{4}} = x^{-4}\), \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} = x^{-\frac{1}{2}}\). Then "bring the power down and reduce the power by one".

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{n}) = nx^{n-1}\) (power rule).
2. For a positive integer \(n\) the proof uses the binomial expansion of \((x+\delta x)^{n}\); every term except \(nx^{n-1}\) contains \(\delta x\) and vanishes in the limit.
3. For a negative integer \(n = -m\), write \(y = \frac{1}{x^{m}}\) and use the expansion of \((x+\delta x)^{m}\).
4. The rule also holds for rational powers (proof left as an exercise in the book), e.g. \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{\frac{2}{3}}) = \frac{2}{3x^{\frac{1}{3}}}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Reducing the power by one in the wrong direction for negative powers: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{-3}) = -3x^{-4}\), not \(-3x^{-2}\). (\(-3 - 1 = -4\).)
2. Forgetting to bring the power down: \(\frac{d}{dx}(x^{5}) = 5x^{4}\), not \(x^{4}\).
3. Applying the rule to \(\frac{1}{x^{2}}\) as if it were \(x^{2}\) in the denominator: first rewrite it as \(x^{-2}\).
4. Using the power rule for \(a^{x}\) (variable in the power). It works only for \(x^{n}\) with a constant power \(n\).
